chapter.title: A share is a slice of a shop

cards.body:
Walk into the bazaar and stop at one stall, say Infosys. The stall has been cut into billions of thin slices, and **one share is one slice**: a real sliver of the buildings, the contracts, the debts and the profits.

The number chalked on the board above the stall is not what the stall is worth. It is only what the last two people agreed on when one slice changed hands.
cards.simpler:
Picture a market with many shops. Pick one, say Infosys. Imagine that shop has been cut into billions of tiny pieces. **One share is one of those pieces.** It is a real piece of the buildings, the deals, the debts and the profits.

The price you see written up for the shop is not what the shop is worth. It is only the price the last buyer and seller agreed on when one piece changed hands.

cards.prompt: A chai stall in the bazaar is cut into 100 slices. This morning 30 people turn up wanting to buy a slice, and only 5 people are willing to sell. What happens to the chalked price?

options.text: It climbs, because buyers have to outbid each other for 5 slices
It drops, because 30 people showing up means the stall is crowded
It stays put until the stall owner decides to change it

whyNot.b: That's what happens when sellers outnumber buyers: they cut their price to find a taker. Here it's the buyers who are many.
whyNot.c: That's a normal shop, not the bazaar: here the company doesn't chalk the price. Buyers and sellers do, every time a slice trades.

cards.reteach: Picture 30 hands up to buy and only 5 slices for sale. The buyers have to outbid each other to get one of those 5, so the agreed price climbs. Flip it, 5 buyers and 30 sellers, and the sellers undercut each other, so it drops.

cards.title: What you actually own
cards.body:
A company that wants money sells slices of itself to the public. Each slice is a *share*: a legal piece of ownership. Infosys has billions of shares, so one share is a very thin slice, but it is yours.

Owning a slice gets you two things. If the company hands out part of its profit, you get your sliver of it: that payout is a *dividend*. And if someone later wants your slice more than you do, you can sell it to them for more than you paid.

It does not get you a say in daily running, a free product, or a promise of your money back. **You own a piece; you are not owed a return.**
cards.simpler:
A company that needs money sells pieces of itself to the public. Each piece is a share: a legal bit of ownership. Infosys has billions, so one share is tiny, but it is yours.

If the company pays out profit, your small part is called a dividend. And you can sell it later, maybe for more than you paid.

It gives no say in running things and no money-back promise. **You own a piece; you are not owed a return.**

cards.title: Four quiet minutes
cards.body:
Say Meera buys 1 share of HDFC Bank at ₹1,650 at 10:00 am. At 10:04 her screen shows ₹1,644. Nothing happened to the bank in those 4 minutes. No branch shut, no loan went bad, no one at head office even looked up.

What happened is that at 10:04 someone wanted to sell more urgently than anyone wanted to buy, and they accepted ₹1,644 to get out. Meera's slice is the same slice. **The price is a record of the last handshake**, not a report card on the bank.
cards.simpler:
Say Meera buys 1 share of HDFC Bank at ₹1,650 at 10:00 am. At 10:04 her screen shows ₹1,644. Nothing happened to the bank in those 4 minutes. No branch shut, no loan went bad, nobody at head office noticed.

At 10:04 someone wanted to sell more badly than anyone wanted to buy, so they accepted ₹1,644. Meera's share is the same share. **The price is a record of the last handshake**, not a report card on the bank.

cards.prompt: Infosys announces a quarter of higher profit, and the share falls 3% that same day. Which explanation uses the bazaar correctly?

options.text: The profit must secretly have been bad, or the price would not fall
More people wanted to sell at that price than buy, perhaps because they had hoped for even more
Someone at the exchange typed the price in wrong

whyNot.a: That's reading the headline backwards: a result can be good and the price still fall, if buyers had already expected better.
whyNot.c: Nobody types the price: it is the number where the last buyer and seller met, so it can't be a typo.

cards.reteach: A price only changes when a buyer and a seller agree on a new number. If more people want out than in, sellers accept less to find a buyer, and the board shows a lower number. The news is just one reason people might want out.

cards.title: How the chalk moves
cards.body:
All day, buyers post the most they will pay and sellers post the least they will take. When one buyer's number meets one seller's number, a trade happens, and that number becomes the new price on the board. Nobody sets it. It is just the latest match.

So the price goes up when buyers must raise their offer to find a willing seller, and down when sellers must lower theirs to find a willing buyer. **More eager buyers than sellers lifts it; more eager sellers than buyers drops it.** That is the whole engine.

Headlines matter only because they change who is eager. A result everyone expected moves nobody, so it moves nothing.
cards.simpler:
All day, buyers name the most they will pay, sellers the least they will take. When a buyer's number meets a seller's, a trade happens and that becomes the new price.

Price rises when buyers must offer more to find a seller, falls when sellers must ask less to find a buyer. **More eager buyers than sellers lifts it; more eager sellers than buyers drops it.**

News only matters by changing who is eager. A result everyone expected moves nothing.

cards.body:
Arjun saw "Reliance falls 2%" and told his sister the company had lost 2% of itself that day, like a wall had come off the stall. The stall was the same stall. What changed was what the last buyer would pay for a slice.

You can spot this mistake whenever someone explains a day's move with a story about the company and never once mentions **who was buying and who was selling**.
cards.simpler:
Arjun saw "Reliance falls 2%" and told his sister the company had lost 2% of itself that day, as if a wall had fallen off the shop. The shop was the same shop. What changed was what the last buyer would pay for one piece of it.

You can spot this mistake whenever someone explains a day's price move with a story about the company and never once mentions **who was buying and who was selling**.

cards.prompt: Your friend texts: "ITC is up 1% today, so ITC must have done something good today." What is the sharpest reply?

options.text: Yes, a price only rises on good news
Not necessarily. It rose because more people wanted to buy at that price than sell. The reason could be anything, or nothing
No, ITC raised its own price because it needs more money

whyNot.a: That's the headline habit: news can nudge buyers, but the price itself only moves on who is buying and selling.
whyNot.c: That's a normal shop, not the bazaar: once shares are out, the company can't chalk the price. Buyers and sellers do.

cards.reteach: Price is a handshake, not a verdict. It rose because at that moment the people wanting to buy outweighed the people wanting to sell. Ask "who was buying?" before "what did the company do?"

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A share is one thin slice of ownership in one company, and it gets you a sliver of any profit paid out plus the right to sell it on, nothing more. **Its price is just the last number a buyer and a seller agreed on**, so it rises when buyers are more eager and falls when sellers are.
cards.simpler: A share is one thin piece of ownership in one company. It gets you a small part of any profit paid out, plus the right to sell it on, and nothing more. **Its price is just the last number a buyer and a seller agreed on.** So it rises when buyers are more eager and falls when sellers are.

cards.body: Tomorrow between 9:15 am and 3:30 pm, search "Infosys share price", note the number, and refresh after 2 minutes. Say out loud which side was more eager in those 2 minutes: buyers or sellers.
cards.simpler: Tomorrow, any time between 9:15 am and 3:30 pm, search "Infosys share price" and write down the number. Wait 2 minutes and refresh the page. Then say out loud **which side was more eager** in those 2 minutes: the buyers or the sellers. If the number went up, buyers were pushing harder. If it went down, sellers were.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in one line why a share rose or fell today, using buyers and sellers instead of headlines.
